title: Enforce a hard maxTokens budget in lore context; add a separate exact-read op for proof evidence
description:
lore context can retain a target larger than maxTokens while marking the result truncated -- current behaviour, not a new failure, but it means a budget is advisory rather than enforced. See LCLI-203 for the existing documented semantics of --max-tokens (omitting it applies no cap; this task is about what happens when it IS supplied and the target still exceeds it).

Proposed: an explicit hard output budget with omitted-record/field metadata, and a separate exact-read operation for proof evidence.

Cross-repo note: the Quest-side half (field and note selection on task view) has already been routed to quest-cli by opum-agent. This task is scoped to Lore's side only.

Source: 2026-09-13 proof-graph inspection (Lore 0.6.0, Quest 0.6.0), read-only against production, recorded as OPAG-120 on opum-agent.

acceptanceCriteria.text: lore context enforces --max-tokens as a hard ceiling: output never exceeds the specified budget
When records/fields are omitted to fit the budget, metadata names what was omitted (record ids and/or fields)
A separate command or flag provides an exact, untruncated read of specific proof evidence, bypassing the token budget entirely
LCLI-203's existing --max-tokens documentation is reconciled with the new hard-budget behavior rather than left contradictory

implementationNotes:
SHARED SHAPE AGREED WITH QUEST-CLI, 2026-09-14. Recorded here because until now this agreement lived
almost entirely in cross-session message traffic, which is not a record. Quest has landed their half
as decision record DEC-3 (`quest decision view DEC-3` in quest-cli's workspace, their PR #79).
LORE STILL OWES A MATCHING RECORD -- write it when this task starts, then exchange record ids with
quest-cli so the two cross-link.

WHY THE TWO TASKS ARE ONE PROBLEM. opum-agent ruled LCLI-478 and quest's QCLI-276 must be designed
together, and quest-cli independently reached the same conclusion before either of us designed
anything. One sentence covers both: A CONSUMER CANNOT ASK FOR PART OF A THING, SO IT TAKES ALL OF IT
OR NOTHING, AND "ALL OF IT" IS UNBOUNDED. Lore's `context` can retain a target larger than maxTokens
and merely mark the result truncated; quest's `task view` always returns the full record and has a
probe task past 1M characters of implementationNotes.

=== THE THREE SEMANTICS. THESE ARE THE AGREEMENT. BOTH PRODUCTS MUST MATCH ON ALL THREE. ===

1. PROJECTION IS OPT-IN AND ADDITIVE. Absent means everything, so today's output is byte-for-byte
   unchanged for every existing caller.

2. A SUPPLIED BOUND IS ENFORCED, NEVER ADVISORY. This is the half to hold hardest, and it is the
   whole defect on lore's side: an advisory budget is the release's own failure mode in another
   costume -- the caller asked for a guarantee and received a suggestion, with no way to tell which
   they got.

3. OMISSION IS REPORTED, NEVER INFERRED. Whatever is dropped, the response SAYS what it dropped. A
   consumer must never have to diff against a full fetch to discover it received a partial one.
   REFINEMENT THAT QUEST ADOPTED VERBATIM AND LORE MUST HONOUR TOO: the omission marker is present
   whenever projection is ACTIVE, including when nothing was omitted (a literal zero) -- not only
   when something was. If it appears only on a capped response, its ABSENCE is ambiguous between
   "nothing was omitted" and "a version that does not report omission", which is the same defect one
   layer down: a marker that cannot announce its own applicability. It costs one integer.

=== WHAT MAY LEGITIMATELY DIFFER, STATED AS A DECISION SO NOBODY READS IT AS DRIFT ===

The flag SPELLING, the UNIT, and the GRANULARITY. Quest bounds by RECORD COUNT (number of notes);
lore bounds by TOKENS across an assembled pack. Those are DIFFERENT KINDS OF BOUND -- a per-field cap
versus a whole-pack budget -- not the same bound in different units, and forcing one spelling to look
consistent would be its own small lie. A consumer learns the three semantics once and then reads each
tool's own flag list. That is a weaker promise than "identical shape" and it is the true one.

=== QUEST'S SIDE, AS LANDED IN DEC-3 (for reference; do not re-derive) ===

 - Scoped NARROWER than a general field-projection DSL, on evidence: their unbounded growth is
   specifically `implementationNotes` and `comments`, not the record as a whole. So `--max-notes N`
   (possibly `--since <ISO>` as a second selector) rather than a column DSL. A plain `--fields a,b,c`
   layers on additively later if a pain point ever appears; there is none today.
 - `notesOmitted: <count>` as a sibling of the shortened array, always present when projection is
   active.
 - Units: record-count.
 - THEIR DEFAULT ALREADY IS THE EXACT READ, so they need no separately-named exact operation --
   projection is purely additive on top of an unbounded default.

=== LORE'S SIDE, STILL TO DESIGN -- AND ONE PIECE IS STRUCTURALLY OURS ALONE ===

`lore context` ASSEMBLES by default and is LOSSY BY DESIGN (selection, ordering, truncation). So
"give me this record verbatim" genuinely is a DIFFERENT OPERATION here, not a flag on the same one --
unlike quest, whose default is already exact. LCLI-478's "separate exact-read op for proof evidence"
is therefore real work on our side and correctly has no counterpart on theirs. A bounded read and an
exact read must be different operations with different names; collapsing them into one operation with
a flag makes the caller who needs fidelity and the caller who needs cheapness share a code path, and
one of them loses.

DEC-3 records that lore-side detail as PENDING, explicitly not absent-by-decision, so a reader of
DEC-3 alone cannot conclude lore declined it. Whichever of us lands second must preserve the same
courtesy in reverse.

See LCLI-203 for the existing documented semantics of --max-tokens (omitting it applies no cap; this
task is about what happens when it IS supplied and the target still exceeds it).

STATUS: NOT BLOCKED ANY MORE ON THE AGREEMENT ITSELF -- the three semantics above are settled and
quest's half is recorded. What remains is lore's own design and implementation. Do not re-open the
three semantics without telling quest-cli; if lore's write-up surfaces something that breaks one,
say so and reopen it jointly rather than diverging quietly.

UNBLOCKED CONFIRMED, 2026-09-14, after the note above was written -- read this second.

quest-cli closed the loop explicitly: DEC-3 is confirmed on BOTH sides, and they have DISPATCHED AN
IMPLEMENTER FOR QCLI-276. Their words: start LCLI-478 whenever it suits, nothing further is owed by
them.

So this task is CLEAR TO START. The note above describes the agreement as settled but was written
while it was still possible that quest would surface something in their write-up that reopened one of
the three semantics. They did not; they are building.

TWO CONSEQUENCES FOR WHOEVER STARTS IT:

1. THE COUNTERPART IS IN FLIGHT, NOT MERELY AGREED. quest's implementation of QCLI-276 is being built
   NOW, against the three semantics recorded above. If lore's design surfaces a problem with any of
   them, that is no longer a cheap conversation -- say so to quest-cli IMMEDIATELY rather than
   working around it locally, because they are writing code against the same agreement and a silent
   divergence is exactly what designing them together was meant to prevent.

2. LORE STILL OWES THE MATCHING DECISION RECORD. quest has DEC-3; lore has nothing durable but this
   task. Write lore's record when the work starts, then exchange record ids with quest-cli so the two
   cross-link. DEC-3 currently marks lore's exact-read half as PENDING rather than absent-by-decision,
   and lore owes them the same courtesy in reverse when its record lands.

LORE'S MATCHING DECISION RECORD IS WRITTEN: DEC-2 in this workspace (`quest decision view DEC-2`), the counterpart to quest-cli's DEC-3. The debt this task's earlier note recorded -- "a cross-link with only one side is half a contract" -- is paid.

WHAT DEC-2 CARRIES: the three semantics verbatim (opt-in and additive; a supplied bound ENFORCED not advisory; omission reported including the zero case), the statement that flag spelling, unit and granularity may legitimately differ because quest bounds by record count and lore by tokens across an assembled pack, and the piece that is structurally lore's alone -- `lore context` assembles and is lossy by design, so an exact read is a DIFFERENT OPERATION here rather than a flag, which is why LCLI-478 has an exact-read half and QCLI-276 does not.

DEC-2 ALSO NAMES WHAT IS STILL PENDING on lore's side -- the hard-budget flag spelling, the exact-read operation's name, and the omission marker's spelling -- explicitly as pending design rather than declined. That is the same courtesy DEC-3 extended to lore when it marked lore's exact-read half PENDING rather than absent, returned in the direction the earlier note said it was owed.

STILL TO DO ON THIS TASK: the implementation. DEC-2 settles the contract, not the code. The four acceptance criteria are untouched by this record.

ONE THING NOT YET DONE AND WORTH NOT FORGETTING: quest-cli has been told DEC-2's id so DEC-3 can name it back. Until DEC-3 carries that reference the cross-link is still one-directional -- from lore to quest -- which is a weaker version of the same defect this record exists to fix.

THE CROSS-LINK IS NOW BIDIRECTIONAL, 2026-09-14. quest-cli replaced DEC-3's one-directional "lore's half is pending, not absent" note with a reference to DEC-2 by name, in their PR #90. So the previous note's open item -- "until DEC-3 carries that reference the cross-link is still one-directional, which is a weaker version of the same defect this record exists to fix" -- is closed, with the caveat that it is closed once their PR #90 lands rather than now. Verify before quoting it as done.

They also confirmed the reciprocal fact worth having on this record: QCLI-276 SHIPPED EXACTLY AS DEC-3 DESCRIBES, and neither their implementation nor their review pushed back on any of the three semantics. So the agreement survived contact with an implementation on one side. Lore's side has not been implemented yet, so it has not been tested the same way -- do not read their result as evidence for ours.

WHAT THIS TASK STILL OWES, unchanged by any of the above: all four acceptance criteria. DEC-2 settles the contract, not the code. The three spellings DEC-2 marks PENDING -- the hard-budget flag, the exact-read operation's name, the omission marker -- are the first design decisions whoever picks this up has to make, and they are pending deliberately rather than by omission.
finalSummary:
Delivered in PR #79, CI run 34918916678 on head e4dc2518 -- all checks SUCCESS or SKIPPED, none failed. That run validates the implementation; the closing commit adds tracker records only.

The contract this implements is DEC-2 in this workspace, the counterpart to quest-cli's DEC-3. DEC-2 marked three spellings pending; all three are decided below and the record now carries them.

AC1 -- lore context enforces --max-tokens as a hard ceiling.
The emitted pack's `tokenEstimate` never exceeds a supplied budget. To stay within it, `context` drops neighbours nearest-first and then, only if the target still does not fit, the target's own `body`. Measured on this repository against ADR-0021 (a ~2900-token concept): `--max-tokens 60` returns 26 tokens with the body omitted; `--max-tokens 9000` returns 2923 with everything present. Omitting the flag applies no cap at all, which is LCLI-203's behaviour and is untouched.

There is deliberately NO new flag, which resolves the first of DEC-2's pending spellings. A second "really mean it" flag would have left `--max-tokens` advisory, and an advisory bound that still exists is the defect wearing a longer name.

AC2 -- omission metadata names what was omitted.
`data.omitted = { records, fields }`. `records` names dropped neighbours by ID, in the order they would have been included -- ids rather than a count, because `shown`/`total` already carry the count and a consumer holding ids can fetch exactly what it is missing. `fields` names any field the budget removed, currently only `target.body`; a field PATH rather than a boolean, so a later droppable field needs no new shape.

BOTH ARRAYS ARE PRESENT WHEN NOTHING WAS DROPPED, which is the half that carries the weight and the half quest adopted verbatim. A marker appearing only on a trimmed pack has an ABSENCE ambiguous between "nothing was dropped" and "a version that does not report omission", so a consumer would have to diff against a full fetch to tell. With no `--max-tokens` the key is absent entirely -- a different, unambiguous statement, because no projection was active. Mutation-tested: removing the zero case fails a test that exists for exactly it.

A budget too small to hold even the target's IDENTITY is refused, exit 6, with required-versus-budget in the message. That reuses `lore agent context`'s existing refusal for the same situation rather than inventing a second spelling; two commands with two answers to one question is how they come to disagree about it.

AC3 -- a separate operation provides an exact, untruncated read.
`lore read <id>` -- the second pending spelling resolved. Frontmatter mapping and full body, verbatim, with NO budget flag at all: passing `--max-tokens` is a usage error rather than an ignored flag, because a flag that is accepted and does nothing is a promise the command does not keep. A test asserts the pairing directly: the same concept whose body `lore context --max-tokens 40` drops is returned whole by `lore read`, so a future change that quietly reunites the two operations fails there.

It is a command rather than a flag because `lore context` assembles and is lossy by design -- selection, ordering, and now a ceiling. That is right for a caller feeding a model a budget it must not exceed and wrong for a caller who needs to quote a document. This is the piece that is structurally lore's alone: quest's default is already exact, so QCLI-276 correctly has no counterpart.

It reports no `backend` (LCLI-499), and the absence is deliberate rather than an oversight: an exact read is always a direct filesystem load, so there is no backend choice to report. A field naming a decision that was never made would be noise pretending to be provenance.

AC4 -- LCLI-203's documentation reconciled rather than left contradictory.
ADR-0015 said "`--max-tokens` is a guardrail, not a guarantee". That was true of the implementation and is precisely what changed, so the paragraph now says what is ACTUALLY approximate -- the chars/4 UNIT, not the enforcement -- and records that the previous wording described the defect. cli-contract and cli-surface carry the enforced semantics and the `omitted` shape. The agent-profile spec no longer points at `lore context <id> --depth 0` as the way to inspect an omitted source, because a depth-0 pack is budgeted too and may drop the very body the agent is trying to read -- a contradiction the change would otherwise have created.

LCLI-203's own sentence -- omitting the flag applies no cap -- stays true and stays.

TWO SCOPE FACTS RECORDED IN DEC-2 RATHER THAN LEFT IMPLICIT. The budget bounds the pack's CONTENT, the same `tokenEstimate` `lore context` has always reported; the omission accounting sits outside it, because the alternative is circular -- listing more dropped ids costs more budget, which drops more neighbours, which lengthens the list. And the refusal shape is borrowed, not invented.

Mutation-tested rather than merely covered: emitting the body regardless of budget, which is the old advisory behaviour, fails 4 tests; reporting omission only when something was omitted fails 1; reporting a count instead of ids fails 1.

Validation: bun test 3042 pass / 1 skip / 0 fail; typecheck clean; lint clean; lore check 78 files, 0 errors, 0 warnings.
